newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - David Hockney reveals his search for light.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - David Hockney reveals his search for light.

text.p: Pop-art pioneer David Hockney left the grey industrial skies of northern Britain in search of light.

Hockney, who rarely speaks to the media, has an exhibition of his new paintings running in London this week. He spoke to Reuters in a brief interview faxed to his old home town of Bradford, and explained his exodus to the west coast of the United States.

"Every morning the sun shines in California," Hockney said in his fax, describing the home where he has lived since leaving Britain in the late 1960s. "I like it, because for the first 20 years of my life it didn't."
Now a leading world art figure, Hockney suffers from hereditary tinnitus and is almost completely deaf.
"He sees the fax machine as a telephone for deaf people," said Anne Davies, manager of the world's largest private collection of Hockney works in the Bradford suburb of Saltaire.

"Technology fascinates David, and this has filtered through to his works," Davies said as she pointed to a huge work consisting of notebook pages faxed across the Atlantic by Hockney with instructions on how to piece them together.
The Saltaire gallery, converted from a 19th century wool mill and which will house Hockney's exhibition when it moves up from London in July, is a mecca for Hockney pilgrims.
Hockney's current show in Britain is his biggest ever commercial exhibition. The last time he exhibited in Britain was at the London's Tate Gallery in 1988.

The London gallery where the current exhibition of 46 brightly coloured flowers and portraits is being held, said the artist had written saying he did not want to be contacted by the media. But he agreed to answer a few questions.
FAX CONVERSATION
In a fax conversation relayed through the London gallery, the Annely Juda Fine Art Gallery, Hockney was asked: "Does this exhibition mark your return to England or are the skies still too grey?"
Gallery owner Annely Juda, who has known the artist since the 1960s, told Reuters Hockney wrote down his fax replies while in London for the opening of the exhibition.
The gently-slanted handwritten reply said of England's skies: "Still slightly grey."
The 59-year-old Hockney said: "Bradford made me search for the sun.
"When the skies are grey, shadows are hardly there. Strong light gives strong shadows."

Some critics of the new exhibition, in which the flower paintings are for sale at prices ranging from 150,000 to 435,000 pounds ($243,000-704,700), have said that Hockney's work became less exciting and less relevant to the pop-art scene after he moved to California.
One art critic on BBC radio this week dismissed the portraits, the prices of which are being negotiated, as "boiled lobsters", a quip often used by pale English people to describe the suntanned.
Jonathan Silver, owner of the Saltaire Gallery, told Reuters it was wrong to pigeon-hole Hockney as a pop-artist. His career spanned a wide variety of styles and mediums.
Hockney's work includes lithographs, etchings, photographs and laser-prints as well as computer generated posters.

Gallery owners say that Silver -- who at 13 bought a small self-portrait by Hockney for two pounds ($3.24) -- gave Hockney the inspiration for his current flower paintings by sending him 59 fresh-cut sunflowers for his birthday.
The London and Saltaire gallery owners said it was a visit to an exhibition by the Dutch master Vermeer in Holland last year which had rekindled Hockney's fascination with light and space.
In his fax, Hockney said of Vermeer: "The physical condition of the colour in his paintings impressed me."
